cards.front: What is an adverse drug reaction (ADR) and how does it differ from an adverse drug event?
cards.back: ADR: a noxious, unintended response suspected to be drug-related, occurring at doses used in humans, that needs treatment, a dose change or caution with future use. Excludes trivial expected effects, overdose and poisoning. Adverse drug event (ADE): any untoward medical occurrence during drug therapy, causation not implied.

cards.front: Compare Type A and Type B adverse drug reactions.
cards.back: Type A (augmented, predictable): exaggerated but qualitatively normal pharmacology; dose-related, common, usually preventable and reversible (side effects, toxicity, withdrawal). Type B (bizarre, unpredictable): not explained by the known action; often not dose-related, rarer, more serious, usually needs drug withdrawal (allergy, idiosyncrasy). Some Type B reactions can be predicted if the genetic basis is known.

cards.front: How is ADR severity graded?
cards.back: Minor: no treatment, antidote or extended stay needed. Moderate: needs change of therapy, specific treatment or stay prolonged by at least a day. Severe: potentially life-threatening, causes permanent damage, or needs intensive care. Lethal: directly or indirectly contributes to death.

cards.front: Type A and Type B adverse drug reactions
cards.text: Type A reactions are {{augmented / predictable}}, usually {{dose-related}}, and mostly preventable. Type B reactions are {{bizarre / unpredictable}}, often {{not dose-related}}, and more {{serious}}.

cards.front: What is a side effect, and why can it often be predicted?
cards.back: An unwanted but often unavoidable pharmacodynamic effect at normal therapeutic doses. It comes from the drug's known pharmacology, so it can be predicted from the drug profile (e.g. dry mouth with atropine, postural hypotension with prazosin). Usually not serious, but can be hazardous: postural hypotension may cause a fall and hip fracture in an elderly patient.

cards.front: Differentiate a secondary effect from a side effect, with examples.
cards.back: A side effect is a direct, unwanted pharmacodynamic action of the drug. A secondary effect is an indirect consequence of the primary action: tetracyclines suppress bacterial flora and open the way to superinfection; corticosteroids weaken host defence, so latent tuberculosis is reactivated.

cards.front: Types of adverse effect and their examples
cards.text: Excess pharmacological action from overdose or prolonged use is a {{toxic effect}}; a low threshold so that toxicity appears at normal doses is {{intolerance}}; a genetically determined abnormal reaction is {{idiosyncrasy}}; an immune-mediated reaction unrelated to pharmacology is {{drug allergy}}.

cards.front: List the practices that minimise adverse drug effects.
cards.back: They can be reduced, never eliminated: (1) avoid inappropriate use for the clinical condition; (2) right dose, route and frequency for the patient; (3) take history of previous drug reactions; (4) take history of allergic diseases (drug allergy is commoner in them); (5) rule out interactions; (6) correct administration technique (e.g. slow i.v. vancomycin); (7) laboratory monitoring (prothrombin time with warfarin, serum levels with lithium).

cards.front: Short note: Idiosyncrasy

points: Genetically determined abnormal reactivity to a chemical
Drug interacts with a unique feature of the individual not found in most people
Restricted to individuals with a particular genotype
Part of Type B (bizarre) reactions: unpredictable, less common, often serious; usually need drug withdrawal

cards.front: Why can the same effect be therapeutic in one patient and a side effect in another? Give examples.
cards.back: Whether an action is wanted depends on the indication. Codeine's constipation is a side effect in cough but the therapeutic aim in traveller's diarrhoea. Depression of AV conduction by digoxin is desired in atrial fibrillation but unwanted in heart failure. Glyceryl trinitrate's vasodilatation relieves angina yet also causes postural hypotension and throbbing headache. Lesson: judge each effect against the reason for giving the drug.

cards.front: Toxic effects: how can overdose be 'relative', and how may toxicity arise from the therapeutic action itself or from another action?
cards.back: Overdose may be absolute (accidental, homicidal, suicidal) or relative: the usual gentamicin dose becomes an overdose in renal failure. Toxicity can be an extension of the therapeutic effect (coma with barbiturates, complete AV block with digoxin, bleeding with heparin) or due to another action (morphine respiratory failure, imipramine arrhythmia, streptomycin vestibular damage on prolonged use). Mechanism: functional change (atropine delirium) or tissue damage. Both are predictable and dose-related.

cards.front: Compare intolerance, idiosyncrasy and drug allergy.
cards.back: Intolerance: typical toxic effect at a therapeutic dose in a person at the sensitive extreme of the dose-response distribution (converse of tolerance), e.g. dystonia after one dose of triflupromazine, ataxia with few doses of carbamazepine, vomiting after one chloroquine tablet. Idiosyncrasy: genetically determined, unusual reaction not seen in most people, e.g. chloramphenicol aplastic anaemia (not dose-related), quinine purpura. Allergy: immune-mediated, needs prior sensitisation and is unrelated to pharmacology. Intolerance is an exaggerated normal action; the other two are qualitatively different.

cards.front: Which Type B reactions can be predicted, and how does genetics explain them?
cards.back: A Type B reaction becomes predictable when its genetic basis is known and a test can identify the individual. Examples: homozygous TPMT variants (about 0.3% of people of European ancestry) risk life-threatening myelosuppression with azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine; HLA-B*5701 carriers get abacavir hypersensitivity; CYP2D6 polymorphisms (absent to ultrarapid activity) change conversion of codeine to morphine. Small premarketing trials contain few carriers of rare variants, so such risks often surface only after marketing.

cards.front: Essay: Classification of adverse drug effects

points: Broad term: any undesirable drug effect
ADR is the narrower term used for monitoring
Side effects: unwanted pharmacodynamic effects at therapeutic doses
Toxic effects: excessive action from overdose or prolonged use
Secondary effects: indirect results of the primary action (e.g. superinfection)
Intolerance: toxic effects at normal doses in low-threshold people
Idiosyncrasy: genetically determined abnormal reaction (e.g. chloramphenicol aplastic anaemia)
Drug allergy and photosensitivity
Gell and Coombs types I to IV
Withdrawal reactions, dependence and addiction
Drug-induced diseases
Mutagenicity, carcinogenicity and teratogenicity
Appropriate indication, dose and route
History of previous reactions and allergy
Screen for interactions and monitor

cards.front: Case synthesis: classify each reaction and say how you would manage it: (a) ototoxicity from the usual gentamicin dose in a patient with renal failure, (b) aplastic anaemia after chloramphenicol, (c) vomiting after one chloroquine tablet.
cards.back: (a) Type A toxic effect from relative overdose: predictable and dose-related; adjust dose to renal function and monitor. (b) Idiosyncrasy, Type B: not dose-related, serious, drug must be withdrawn; cannot be prevented by dose reduction. (c) Intolerance: a low-threshold individual shows a usual toxic effect at therapeutic dose; stop or substitute. Principle: Type A is managed by dose and monitoring, Type B by withdrawal and avoidance in future.

cards.front: Define pharmacovigilance (WHO, 2002).
cards.back: The science and activities concerned with detecting, assessing, understanding and preventing adverse effects or other drug-related problems. Main aim: reduce drug-related harm and support rational use. Core activities: post-marketing surveillance and spontaneous reporting, drug alerts and advisories, and regulatory label changes or withdrawal.

cards.front: What do dechallenge and rechallenge mean in causality assessment?
cards.back: Dechallenge: the event subsides after the drug is stopped (supports causation). Rechallenge: the event recurs when the drug is given again after it had resolved (strongly supports causation). Rechallenge is often unethical or dangerous, so it is avoided.

cards.front: Grades of causality of an ADR
cards.text: Causality is graded {{definite}} (proven), {{probable}} (drug is the likely cause), {{possible}} (drug or other causes could be responsible) and {{doubtful}} (drug unlikely but not excluded).

cards.front: Why are premarketing trials not enough to establish drug safety?
cards.back: They are small (median about 467 patients in pivotal trials of drugs approved 2015-17), short (median about 24 weeks; only about 46% had a trial of at least 6 months) and restricted to selected patients. So uncommon, delayed or genotype-related reactions are missed. Example: terfenadine was studied in about 5000 patients before approval but 7.5 million were exposed before its withdrawal. Hence postmarketing surveillance is needed.

cards.front: Pharmacovigilance Programme of India
cards.text: PvPI began in {{2010}} under the Ministry of Health; CDSCO and the {{Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad}} (national coordination centre) run it; the international collaborating centre is the {{Uppsala Monitoring Centre}}.

cards.front: List the limitations of spontaneous adverse event reporting.
cards.back: (1) Marked under-reporting (median about 94% across 12 countries), varying with media coverage, litigation and time on market. (2) Denominator unknown, so incidence cannot be calculated or compared between drugs. (3) Reports often incomplete (history, co-medication, cause of death, start date). (4) Cannot detect a small-to-moderate rise in a common event, which needs controlled studies. (5) Signals are hard to separate from noise and need further evaluation.

cards.front: When are single case reports most useful for inferring that a drug caused an event?
cards.back: When the event is otherwise rare, has few other risk factors, follows exposure closely in time, and the drug carries a large excess risk. Examples: anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, cerivastatin rhabdomyolysis. Then no other method detects the adverse effect as fast or cheaply. For common events, such reports cannot establish causality.

cards.front: Essay: Pharmacovigilance: purpose, methods and role in India

points: WHO (2002) definition: detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse effects or other drug-related problems
Aim: reduce drug-related harm; supports rational use and regulation
Voluntary (spontaneous) reporting, e.g. UK yellow card; reporting is minimal in India
Under-reporting is large: GG14 cites a median under-reporting rate of about 94% across 12 countries (older KDT8 figure: only about 10% of ADRs reported voluntarily)
Prescription event monitoring, record linkage, cohort and case-control studies, case reports
Drug alerts, medical letters and advisories
Label changes, restrictions, warnings or withdrawal by the regulator
Uppsala Monitoring Centre (Sweden): WHO international collaborating centre (VigiBase)
India: PvPI, started 2010 by the Health Ministry through CDSCO and the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad (National Coordination Centre)
ADR monitoring centres in medical colleges and hospitals; peripheral, regional and zonal centres; National Pharmacovigilance Advisory Committee
Causality: WHO scale, Naranjo algorithm
Severity: modified Hartwig scale
Under-reporting; no denominator, so incidence cannot be calculated
Dramatic, immediate reactions reported more than delayed ones

cards.front: Spontaneous reports show a possible signal that a drug raises the rate of a common event such as myocardial infarction. How should it be handled?
cards.back: Spontaneous systems cannot show a small-to-moderate rise in a common event (no denominator, background events are expected, reports incomplete), so the signal only triggers evaluation. Next step: controlled studies, either observational pharmacoepidemiology (e.g. FDA Sentinel, which draws on electronic data of over 100 million people) or a postmarketing trial. Observational studies are limited by costly, slow access to data and by confounding. Rosiglitazone showed why: approved on glycaemic trials, later meta-analysis suggested raised MI risk.

cards.front: Short note: Postmarketing drug safety (approaches and regulatory response)

points: Premarketing trials small, short and in selected patients
Withdrawals followed wide exposure, e.g. terfenadine, fenfluramine, dexfenfluramine, mibefradil, bromfenac
Case reports and spontaneous systems: foundation (FAERS receives over 2 million reports a year; MedWatch for voluntary reporting, mandatory for manufacturers)
Controlled studies: observational pharmacoepidemiology (Sentinel System, over 100 million people's electronic data) and postmarketing trials
Communication: label change, boxed warning, drug safety communication
REMS
Withdrawal from market (drastic; weigh risk, benefit and alternatives)
QT prolongation withdrawals (terfenadine, astemizole, grepafloxacin, cisapride) raised QT testing requirements
Valvular toxicity of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine, and sibutramine, led to stricter CV requirements for antiobesity drugs

cards.front: Gell and Coombs Type I hypersensitivity: mechanism and clinical picture?
cards.back: IgE antibodies fixed to mast cells and basophils; on re-exposure, antigen cross-links IgE and mediators (histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, PAF) are released. Immediate reaction within minutes to hours: urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, rhinitis and anaphylaxis.

cards.front: Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity types
cards.text: Type I is {{IgE}}-mediated via {{mast cells}}; Type II is {{cytotoxic}} via {{IgG or IgM}} antibodies; Type III is {{immune complex}}-mediated (serum sickness); Type IV is {{T-lymphocyte}}-mediated (contact dermatitis).

cards.front: What are the cardinal features of drug allergy and why is prior exposure needed?
cards.back: Features: manifestations unrelated to the drug's pharmacology; resemble food or protein allergy; severity poorly related to dose; only a few recipients; prior sensitisation needed; positive dechallenge and rechallenge even with a small dose. Drugs are small molecules that act as haptens, becoming antigenic only after binding to body proteins; the immune system needs a latent period (at least 1-2 weeks) to make antibody or sensitised T cells, so the first exposure sensitises and a later one reacts.

cards.front: Type II, III and IV drug hypersensitivity: mechanism and typical manifestations?
cards.back: Type II (cytolytic): IgG or IgM binds drug-tissue cell complex, complement activates, cell lysis: thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, haemolysis. Type III (Arthus-like): circulating IgG immune complexes deposit on vessel walls and tissues, causing inflammation: rash, serum sickness. Type IV (delayed): sensitised T lymphocytes release lymphokines, 2-3 days: contact dermatitis, some rashes, fever, photosensitisation.

cards.front: Which drugs most often cause allergic reactions?
cards.back: Penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, quinolones, metronidazole, abacavir, antitubercular drugs, phenothiazines, aspirin, indomethacin, carbamazepine, allopurinol, ACE inhibitors, methyldopa, hydralazine, local anaesthetics.

cards.front: First-line emergency treatment of drug-induced anaphylaxis?
cards.back: Adrenaline intramuscularly (adult 0.5 mg of 1:1000 solution; lower doses for children), repeated every 5-10 minutes if needed. Supportive steps: recline, high-flow oxygen, resuscitation if required. Add H1 antihistamine and IV hydrocortisone for severe or recurrent cases. Do not give IV adrenaline unless shock is life-threatening, and then dilute it.

cards.front: Phototoxic vs photoallergic drug reactions: which UV band and which mechanism?
cards.back: Phototoxic: a photoactivated drug or metabolite damages tissue directly; sunburn-like reaction, fast onset, UVB (290-320 nm); more common. Photoallergic: an immune response, eczema-like reaction that may persist, UVA (320-400 nm); small doses can trigger it. Tetracyclines (demeclocycline) are classic phototoxic agents.

cards.front: Short note: Drug allergy (hypersensitivity)

points: Immune-mediated reaction unrelated to the drug's pharmacology
Occurs in a small fraction of users; not dose-related
Needs prior sensitisation: latent period of at least 1-2 weeks after first exposure
Drug or metabolite usually acts as a hapten; cross-sensitivity among chemically related drugs
Type I: IgE, immediate (anaphylaxis, urticaria, asthma)
Type II: cytotoxic, IgG/IgM (haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis)
Type III: immune complex (serum sickness, vasculitis)
Type IV: T-cell mediated, delayed (contact dermatitis)
Penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, quinolones, metronidazole, antitubercular drugs, abacavir
Phenothiazines, aspirin, indomethacin, carbamazepine, allopurinol, ACE inhibitors, methyldopa, hydralazine, local anaesthetics
Stop the drug at once; mild rashes often settle alone
H1 antihistamines for some type I reactions; adrenaline i.m. for anaphylaxis
Glucocorticoids for severe or prolonged reactions
Skin or intranasal tests help only for type I and give false positives and negatives

cards.front: Why is adrenaline the key drug in anaphylaxis, and why is it given i.m. and not i.v.?
cards.back: Adrenaline counters the mediator-driven bronchospasm, vasodilatation and angioedema and is the only life-saving measure: 0.5 mg (0.5 ml of 1 in 1000) i.m. in an adult, repeated every 5-10 minutes if needed. It is not given i.v. because it can itself be dangerous; only if shock is life-threatening, and then diluted. Antihistamines and hydrocortisone are adjuncts, not substitutes, since antihistamines help only some type I features.

cards.front: Which drug class works in type II, III and IV drug reactions, and how is a mild drug rash managed?
cards.back: Glucocorticoids are the only drugs effective in types II, III and IV. First step in all drug allergy: stop the offending drug. Mild rashes usually subside alone; H1 antihistamines relieve itching, urticaria and rhinitis in some type I reactions and some rashes; calamine lotion or mild topical steroid for local relief. Skin and intranasal tests help only for type I and can be falsely positive or negative.

cards.front: Short note: Photosensitivity reactions

points: Drug-induced sensitisation of skin to UV radiation, two types
Drug or metabolite accumulates in skin, absorbs light, damages tissue
Sunburn-like: erythema, oedema, blistering; fast onset, shorter course; then hyperpigmentation and desquamation
UVB (290-320 nm); more common; tetracyclines (demeclocycline) classic
Cell-mediated immune response; eczema-like contact dermatitis picture that may persist
Avoid sun; sunscreen SPF 15-60
Soothing lotions (calamine), wet dressings, mild topical steroids for phototoxicity; strong topical or systemic steroids for photoallergy

points: Immune-mediated, stereotyped reaction unrelated to the drug's pharmacology; needs prior sensitisation; drug acts as hapten
I: IgE on mast cells, histamine, LT-C4 and D4, PAF; minutes to hours; urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis
II: IgG or IgM cytolysis; thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis, haemolysis
III: immune complexes; serum sickness, rash, vasculitis
IV: T cell, 2-3 days; contact dermatitis, fever, photosensitisation
Penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides and others
Stop the drug
Anaphylaxis: reclining position, oxygen, i.m. adrenaline 0.5 mg repeated at 5-10 minutes, H1 antihistamine and hydrocortisone as adjuncts
Glucocorticoids the only effective drugs in types II-IV
Mild rashes settle alone
Phototoxic (UVB) versus photoallergic (UVA)
Skin tests help only type I and are unreliable
History of allergic diseases and prior reactions

cards.front: Compare three patients: (a) wheeze and urticaria minutes after penicillin, (b) fever, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy and rash in week 2 of a sulfonamide, (c) eczema 2-3 days after a topical drug. Name the type, mediator and treatment.
cards.back: (a) Type I: IgE on mast cells; adrenaline i.m. first, antihistamine and steroid as adjuncts. (b) Type III (serum sickness): circulating IgG immune complexes; stop the drug, glucocorticoid. (c) Type IV: sensitised T lymphocytes and lymphokines; stop the drug, glucocorticoid (topical or systemic). Key: only type I is quick and adrenaline-responsive; glucocorticoids are the only effective drugs in II, III and IV.

cards.front: Which periods of pregnancy are most relevant for drug teratogenicity?
cards.back: Three stages: (1) fertilisation and implantation, conception to day 17: failure of pregnancy, often unnoticed; (2) organogenesis, days 18 to 55: most vulnerable, structural malformations; (3) growth and development, day 56 onwards: developmental and functional defects, e.g. ACE inhibitors (hypoplasia of lungs and kidneys), NSAIDs (premature closure of ductus arteriosus), androgens/progestins (masculinisation of female foetus), antithyroid drugs and lithium (foetal goitre).

cards.front: What lesson came from the thalidomide disaster?
cards.back: Thalidomide, marketed in 1957 as a sedative and anti-morning-sickness drug, taken in the first trimester caused thousands of babies to be born with phocomelia (seal-like limbs) and other defects (1958-61). It was banned worldwide. The disaster focused attention on teratogenicity testing; thalidomide is now marketed again only for restricted use, e.g. as an adjuvant in cancer chemotherapy.

cards.front: Teratogenic drugs and their defects
cards.text: ACE inhibitors cause {{hypoplasia of organs}} (especially lungs and kidneys); valproate causes {{spina bifida}} and other neural tube defects; warfarin causes a {{depressed nose}} with eye and hand defects; antithyroid drugs cause foetal {{goitre}}.

cards.front: Define teratogenicity, mutagenicity and carcinogenicity.
cards.back: Teratogenicity: capacity of a drug to cause foetal abnormalities when given to the pregnant mother. Mutagenicity: capacity to cause genetic defects, possibly heritable. Carcinogenicity: capacity to cause cancer. Reactive intermediates (often from oxidation) bind covalently to DNA; if proto-oncogenes or inhibitors of their transcription are altered, a tumour can result. Drugs implicated include anticancer drugs, radioisotopes, estrogens and tobacco.

cards.front: Why is the placenta no protection, and why is the embryo so vulnerable?
cards.back: The placenta is not a strict barrier: any drug crosses to some degree. The embryo is a highly dynamic biological system and, unlike adults, drug effects on it are often irreversible. Teratogenic risk is judged against the spontaneous background of about 2% of pregnancies with congenital anomalies.

cards.front: Why does the same drug cause different harm depending on the stage of pregnancy?
cards.back: Foetal harm depends on drug and timing. Days 0-17: failure of pregnancy, often unnoticed. Days 18-55 (organogenesis): structural malformation. From day 56: functional and growth defects, e.g. ACE inhibitors (lung, kidney hypoplasia), NSAIDs (ductus arteriosus closes early), androgens and progestins (virilisation of female foetus), antithyroid drugs and lithium (goitre). Exposure also depends on maternal blood level and duration.

cards.front: Group the human teratogens by type of effect.
cards.back: Structural malformations: thalidomide (phocomelia), methotrexate (cleft palate, hydrocephalus), warfarin (depressed nose, eye and hand defects), phenytoin (hypoplastic phalanges, cleft lip/palate), valproate (neural tube defects), isotretinoin (craniofacial, heart, CNS). Growth or functional: ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, lithium, antithyroid drugs, tetracyclines (teeth, bone), alcohol (foetal alcohol syndrome). Delayed: stilboestrol (vaginal carcinoma in teenage daughters). Antiepileptics (phenytoin, phenobarbitone, carbamazepine, valproate) form a notable group.

cards.front: How did risk labelling for pregnancy change, and why is the old system criticised?
cards.back: The old FDA letter grades A (safe) to X (contraindicated) became outdated as evidence on teratogenicity accumulated, and their usefulness was questioned. In 2015 the FDA Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule replaced them with narrative labelling on pregnancy, lactation and reproductive potential. KDT advises avoiding all drugs in pregnancy unless there is a compelling reason, whatever the assigned category.

cards.front: A pregnant woman takes valproate for epilepsy, an ACE inhibitor for hypertension and an antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism. What are the foetal risks and your advice?
cards.back: Valproate: neural tube defects (spina bifida) and other defects; ACE inhibitor: organ hypoplasia (lung, kidney) and foetal loss; antithyroid drug: foetal goitre. Advice: review every drug, avoid unnecessary ones whatever the category, use a drug only where a compelling indication exists, and give folate, which lowers neural tube defects. Which risk applies depends on the stage of exposure.

cards.front: Distinguish drug dependence from drug addiction.
cards.back: Dependence (neuroadaptation; formerly 'physical dependence'): an altered physiological state needing continued drug presence; stopping it causes a characteristic withdrawal syndrome (opioids, barbiturates, alcohol, benzodiazepines). Addiction (formerly 'psychological dependence'): compulsive use with overwhelming involvement, despite known harm, with frequent relapse. Amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis and LSD cause addiction with little or no dependence; nalorphine causes dependence without addiction.

cards.front: Give two examples of withdrawal reactions after abrupt cessation of a drug.
cards.back: Clonidine: rebound hypertension, restlessness and sympathetic overactivity. Beta-blockers: worsened angina or myocardial infarction. Corticosteroids: acute adrenal insufficiency. Antiepileptics: increased seizure frequency. Prevention: taper gradually.

cards.front: What is tolerance, and how does it relate to dependence?
cards.back: Tolerance: need for a higher dose to get a given response; a common adaptive biological phenomenon (mechanisms include receptor desensitisation, internalisation, down-regulation and compensatory homeostatic adaptation). Drugs taken repeatedly for gratification also cause adaptive changes: tolerance (dose escalation) and a disturbed physiological balance when the drug is absent, which is dependence with withdrawal. Tolerance is the converse of intolerance.

cards.front: What is reinforcement and why do some routes and drugs have more abuse potential?
cards.back: Reinforcement is the drug's ability to produce effects the user enjoys and so to induce drug-seeking. Opioids and cocaine are strong reinforcers, benzodiazepines weak. The faster the drug acts, the more reinforcing: inhaled and intravenous drugs give an intense rapid effect, which raises abuse risk.

cards.front: Dependence terminology
cards.text: {{Dependence}} means a withdrawal syndrome on stopping; {{addiction}} means compulsive use with overwhelming involvement and relapse; {{habituation}} is milder involvement without dependence (tea, coffee); {{abuse}} is use deviating from approved medical and social patterns.

cards.front: Short note: Drug dependence, addiction and abuse

points: Dependence (neuroadaptation): withdrawal syndrome on stopping
Addiction: compulsive use with overwhelming involvement despite harm; relapse common
Habituation: milder involvement without dependence (tea, coffee, tobacco, social drinking); term best avoided
Abuse: self-medication deviating from approved medical and social patterns; for regulators, any use of an illicit drug
Dependence: opioids, barbiturates, alcohol, benzodiazepines
Addiction with little/no dependence: amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, LSD
Dependence without addiction: nalorphine
Strong reinforcers: opioids, cocaine; weak: benzodiazepines
Faster-acting routes (inhaled, i.v.) are most reinforcing
Continuous use: opioids, alcohol, sedatives
Occasional use for a 'high': cocaine, amphetamines, psychedelics, cannabis, solvents, binge drinking

cards.front: Short note: Designer drugs (new psychoactive substances)

points: Novel psychoactive drugs that keep entering the illicit market
Trends change constantly, so surveillance sources track novel illicit drugs
Synthetic cannabinoids and synthetic cathinones (e.g. ethylone) are the most common classes of new psychoactive substances
Opioids, phenethylamines, tryptamines, benzodiazepines and piperazines are also of concern

cards.front: Why do clonidine, beta-blockers, corticosteroids and antiepileptics cause problems on abrupt stopping, and how is it prevented?
cards.back: Chronic use causes adaptive changes; abrupt withdrawal removes the drug and the condition worsens or rebounds: severe hypertension and sympathetic overactivity (clonidine), worsened angina or myocardial infarction (beta-blockers), acute adrenal insufficiency (corticosteroids), more seizures (antiepileptics). Prevention is gradual withdrawal by tapering.

cards.front: Compare dependence and addiction using examples.
cards.back: Opioids, barbiturates, alcohol and benzodiazepines cause dependence (withdrawal syndrome). Amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis and LSD cause addiction with little or no dependence, so dependence is not essential for addiction. Nalorphine causes dependence without addiction. Relapse after withdrawal is typical of addiction, and the faster-acting routes reinforce it most.

cards.front: Essay: Drug dependence, addiction and abuse

points: Mood-altering drugs are used repeatedly for euphoria, recreation and escape; terms changed (physical dependence now dependence; psychological dependence now addiction)
Altered physiological state needing continued drug; characteristic withdrawal syndrome
Opioids, barbiturates, alcohol and benzodiazepines
Compulsive use, overwhelming involvement despite harm, relapse
Amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, LSD; dependence not essential
Dose escalation from adaptive changes
Strong reinforcers opioids and cocaine; fast routes more reinforcing
Habituation, abuse
Continuous use (opioids, alcohol, sedatives); occasional use (cocaine, amphetamines, psychedelics, cannabis, solvents, binge drinking)
Clonidine, beta-blockers, corticosteroids, antiepileptics: taper gradually
New psychoactive substances: synthetic cannabinoids and cathinones are most common

cards.front: Compare three patients: an opioid user, a cocaine user and a hypertensive taking clonidine. Each stops the drug suddenly. What happens and why?
cards.back: Opioid: dependence, so a characteristic withdrawal syndrome. Cocaine: addiction with little or no dependence, so strong craving and relapse but minimal withdrawal. Clonidine: not a dependence-producing drug, but adaptive changes cause rebound hypertension, restlessness and sympathetic overactivity. Common thread: adaptation to the drug; for clonidine the answer is to taper.

cards.front: Drug-induced diseases and their causative drugs
cards.text: NSAIDs and corticosteroids cause {{peptic ulcer}}; phenothiazines cause {{parkinsonism}}; isoniazid causes {{hepatitis}}; hydralazine causes {{drug-induced lupus}}.

cards.front: What is a poison, a toxin, and what separates a drug from a poison?
cards.back: Poison: a substance that endangers life by severely affecting vital functions; a poison of biological origin is a toxin; poisoning is harmful effect of a chemical on a biological system. The dose separates drug from poison. Poisons include household, environmental and industrial chemicals and insecticides, not only drugs. Specific antidotes (receptor antagonists, chelators) exist for only a few.

cards.front: What are the general steps in acute poisoning, in order?
cards.back: (1) Resuscitation: airway and breathing (oxygen), circulation (fluids, pressors, pacing), stop seizures (i.v. lorazepam), temperature, blood sugar (dextrose). (2) Termination of exposure, started at the same time: fresh air, remove clothing, wash skin and eyes, emesis or lavage for ingested poisons. (3) Prevent absorption: activated charcoal. (4) Hasten elimination. (5) Specific antidote if available. Resuscitation comes first because poisoning often causes coma with loss of airway reflexes.

cards.front: Activated charcoal in poisoning
cards.text: Activated charcoal is given as {{20-40 g (or 1 g/kg)}} in 200 ml water. It does not adsorb {{strong acids and alkalis}}, metallic salts, iodine, {{cyanide}}, alcohol or hydrocarbons, and is avoided in {{ileus or obstruction}}.

cards.front: Short note: Drug-induced diseases (iatrogenic disease)

points: Functional disease caused by a drug that persists after the drug is stopped and cleared
Peptic ulcer with NSAIDs and corticosteroids
Parkinsonism with antipsychotics (phenothiazines)
Hepatitis with isoniazid
Drug-induced lupus with hydralazine or procainamide
Immune injury (hypersensitivity)
Direct tissue toxicity
Interference with normal physiology (e.g. dopamine blockade)
Often mistaken for a new disease; a drug history is essential
Some are irreversible or slow to resolve

cards.front: Short note: Nephrotoxic drugs

points: Aminoglycosides, tetracyclines (except doxycycline), sulfonamides (crystalluria), vancomycin
Cyclosporine increases nephrotoxicity when combined with other nephrotoxic drugs

cards.front: Short note: Toxicokinetics and enhanced elimination of poisons

points: Toxicokinetics: the pharmacokinetics of a drug under conditions that produce toxicity
Overdose can alter absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination
Time to peak concentration sets how long asymptomatic patients must be observed
Weak acids are trapped as ions in alkaline urine, so alkalinising urine speeds elimination of phenobarbital, chlorpropamide and salicylates
US clinical toxicologists favour urine alkalinisation first-line only for moderately severe salicylate poisoning not needing haemodialysis
Multiple-dose activated charcoal moves drug from blood across the gut wall onto charcoal in the lumen, enhancing elimination of some drugs
Haemodialysis suits drugs with low molecular weight, low volume of distribution and high water solubility

cards.front: When are emesis and lavage contraindicated or pointless, and why?
cards.back: Contraindicated in coma or an unstable patient, in kerosene poisoning (vomiting risks aspiration into the lungs), and in corrosive and CNS stimulant poisoning. Not recommended after 2 hours, when the dose is non-toxic, or when the patient has already vomited. Decontamination is therefore selective.

cards.front: Which poisons are removed by urinary alkalinisation or haemodialysis, and why is forced diuresis no longer used?
cards.back: Alkalinisation traps weak acids as ions (phenobarbital, chlorpropamide, salicylates); the American Academy of Clinical Toxicologists recommends it first-line only for moderately severe salicylate poisoning that does not meet haemodialysis criteria. Haemodialysis suits low molecular weight, small volume of distribution and high water solubility: phenobarbitone, carbamazepine, valproate, lithium, salicylate, theophylline. Forced diuresis (furosemide, mannitol) is generally abandoned: poisons cleared by hepatic metabolism are not helped and fluid overload and electrolyte imbalance outweigh benefit.

cards.front: Short note: Management of acute poisoning

points: Airway and ventilation (oxygen, artificial respiration)
Maintain BP and heart: fluids, pressors, pacing, defibrillation
Control seizures (i.v. lorazepam); maintain temperature and blood sugar
Fresh air for inhaled poisons; remove clothing, wash skin and eyes
Emesis or gastric lavage only in few cases: not in coma, unstable patients, kerosene, corrosives or CNS stimulants
Not useful if presentation is beyond 2 h, dose is non-toxic, or patient has vomited
Activated charcoal 20-40 g (or 1 g/kg) in water
Does not adsorb strong acids/alkalis, metallic salts, iodine, cyanide, caustics, alcohol, hydrocarbons, organic solvents
Avoid with ileus or obstruction, or after 2 h
Forced diuresis and urinary pH change: generally not used now (fluid and electrolyte risk)
Haemodialysis for phenobarbitone, carbamazepine, valproate, lithium, salicylate, theophylline
Specific antidotes exist for only a few poisons

cards.front: Comatose patient, phenobarbitone overdose 3 hours ago, unstable. Outline management.
cards.back: Resuscitate first: secure airway, ventilate, support blood pressure, control seizures, check glucose and temperature. No emesis or lavage (coma, unstable, over 2 hours). No activated charcoal after 2 hours, and none with ileus or obstruction. Urinary alkalinisation is possible (weak acid trapping); forced diuresis is not used. Haemodialysis is more efficacious for phenobarbitone, so it is the stronger option in a severe case. Specific antidotes exist for only a few poisons, so supportive care.

cards.front: Which kinds of specific antidote exist in poisoning, and why is supportive care still essential?
cards.back: Specific antidotes are of three kinds: receptor antagonists, chelating agents and specific antibodies. They exist for only a few poisons, so for most poisons general supportive and symptomatic treatment is all that can be done. Supportive care also matters when an antidote exists, because the antidote reverses only one mechanism, not the airway, circulation and seizure problems already present.

cards.front: What is randomisation in a clinical trial, and what is its role in limiting bias?
cards.back: Subjects are allocated to study groups by chance, using a random-number table or computer. It is one of the two basic strategies for minimising bias; the other is blinding (concealment of treatment).

cards.front: How does stratified randomisation differ from simple randomisation, and when is it used?
cards.back: Patients are first grouped by a key variable (age, sex, disease severity or another patient factor) and then randomised within each group. It is used when such a factor could distort the comparison between treatment groups.

cards.front: Short note: Randomisation vs stratification

points: Both are methods of allocating subjects in controlled trials
Both aim to reduce bias in comparing groups
Allocation purely by chance (random table or computer)
One of the two basic bias-limiting strategies, with blinding
Subjects grouped by key variables such as age, sex or disease severity
Randomisation then carried out within each group
Stratification protects against imbalance of a known patient factor
Stratified randomisation is an addition to, not a replacement for, randomisation

cards.front: Adverse drug event (ADE) vs adverse drug reaction (ADR): which needs a suspected causal link to the drug?
cards.back: ADR: a noxious response suspected to be due to the drug, at normal doses, needing treatment or dose change; trivial effects, poisoning and overdose are excluded. ADE: any untoward occurrence during treatment, with no causal link needed. ADEs are recorded first and causality is judged later in pooled data.

cards.front: Short note: Underreporting of adverse drug reactions

points: Spontaneous reporting misses most events; median underreporting about 94% across 12 countries
So spontaneous data cannot give true event frequency
Media coverage of a drug or event
Litigation
Time since the drug was marketed
Reporting patterns change unpredictably over a drug's life cycle
Number of patients actually exposed is hard to estimate
Without it the rate of an event cannot be calculated

cards.front: Why is an idiosyncratic reaction unpredictable? Give the chloramphenicol example.
cards.back: It depends on a peculiarity of the patient, not on the drug's known action (Type B). Chloramphenicol aplastic anaemia is rare (about 1 in 40,000), not dose-related, probably genetic, and often fatal.

cards.front: Short note: Institutional review board (ethics committee)

points: Independent body that scrutinises and approves a trial before it starts
Called an independent ethics committee or IRB
All human experiments need its approval
Weighs safety, ethics and scientific value of the study
Receives the key preclinical data and protocol, per the drug development dossier
Trials follow Good Clinical Practice (GCP)
In India, ICMR ethical guidelines for biomedical research (2006)
Written informed consent from each subject

cards.front: Which blood cell lines does drug-induced bone marrow depression affect?
cards.back: Granulocytes (granulocytopenia, agranulocytosis), platelets (thrombocytopenia), and in severe cases aplastic anaemia. Bone marrow depression is the most serious toxicity of such drugs and often limits the dose.

cards.front: Short note: Drug-induced agranulocytosis

points: Fall in granulocytes from bone-marrow depression (dose-related) or an idiosyncratic reaction
Infections and bleeding are the usual complications
Chloramphenicol: most prominent antibiotic cause of agranulocytosis and aplastic anaemia
Clozapine: agranulocytosis more common than with other antipsychotics
Carbamazepine: rare; mild leucopenia more common
Procainamide: rare
Dapsone: rare complication
Anticancer drugs: marrow depression is their most serious toxicity

cards.front: Carbamazepine is dose-related neurotoxic. Name its effects, and how extended-release tablets help.
cards.back: Sedation, dizziness, vertigo, diplopia and ataxia. Extended-release tablets avoid high peaks in plasma level, so the neurological symptoms are less frequent.

cards.front: Why does isoniazid cause neuropathy, and why is pyridoxine given with it?
cards.back: Isoniazid hampers the conversion of pyridoxine to its active phosphate and increases its urinary loss. Prophylactic pyridoxine (10 mg/day) prevents the neurotoxicity; 100 mg/day is used to treat it.

cards.front: Which patients need prophylactic pyridoxine with isoniazid?
cards.back: Diabetics, chronic alcoholics, malnourished, pregnant or lactating women, HIV-infected patients, and anyone on high-dose isoniazid. Why: isoniazid blocks activation of pyridoxine and increases its urinary loss.

cards.front: Short note: Drugs causing neurotoxicity

points: Mostly dose-related toxic effects on the nervous system
Often prevented or reduced by dose timing or a co-drug
Carbamazepine: sedation, dizziness, vertigo, diplopia, ataxia
Isoniazid: peripheral neuropathy, prevented by pyridoxine
Cycloserine: neuropsychiatric effects in about half of users; seizures and psychosis possible; pyridoxine 100 mg/day helps
Terizidone: reported less neurotoxic substitute for cycloserine
Local anaesthetics: neurotoxicity blamed with high or repeated doses
Pyridoxine prophylaxis for high-risk groups
Cycloserine is contraindicated in mental illness or seizures

cards.front: Which type of ADR is dose-related and mostly preventable?
cards.back: Type A (predictable, augmented) reactions. They follow the drug's known pharmacology, are more common with multiple drugs and in the elderly, and are mostly preventable and reversible.

cards.front: Short note: Preventable adverse drug reactions

points: Type A (augmented) reactions: dose-related, mostly preventable and reversible
Type B reactions are not dose-related and are not preventable by dose change
Multiple drug therapy
Elderly patients
Rational prescribing: right drug, dose and duration
Check the drug history before prescribing
Tell the patient about common side effects, precautions and warnings, without discouraging use
Lab tests when needed, e.g. leucocyte count with anticancer drugs

cards.front: Short note: Thalidomide and its analogues

points: Introduced for morning sickness in pregnancy; taken early in pregnancy
Caused phocomelia and other defects; over 10,000 children affected (1957-61)
Lesson: rare serious ADRs appear only after wide clinical use
Immunomodulator and anti-inflammatory: used for erythema nodosum leprosum, probably through its anti-inflammatory property
Antitumour use, e.g. multiple myeloma with melphalan and dexamethasone
Cancer-associated cachexia: reported benefit

cards.front: Why is thalidomide still used despite its teratogenicity?
cards.back: It was reintroduced after the ban as an immunomodulator and anti-inflammatory drug, e.g. in erythema nodosum leprosum and in some cancers. Its teratogenic risk is the reason for restricted use.

cards.front: Which drugs can cause insomnia as an adverse effect? List them.
cards.back: Nicotine replacement therapy; tofacitinib; caffeine and theophylline (more so at high doses); systemic glucocorticoids; tizanidine; selegiline (via its amphetamine metabolite); amantadine; amisulpride; amphetamines (high doses); older H1 antihistamines (stimulant effect in some). Why: theophylline causes insomnia at higher doses, selegiline's amphetamine metabolite causes it, and amisulpride's common side effects include insomnia and agitation.

cards.front: Underreporting of ADRs: what is it and why does it matter?
cards.back: Most adverse drug reactions never reach the national reporting system. Hidden cases mean the real risk of a drug stays unknown after approval.

cards.front: Short note: ADR, PvPI 2025 theme and underreporting

points: Harmful, unintended response to a drug given at normal doses for prophylaxis, diagnosis or therapy
Type A: dose-related, predictable; Type B: idiosyncratic, unpredictable
Reporting to PvPI supports causality assessment and regulatory action
Fifth National Pharmacovigilance Week, run by IPC as the national coordination centre of PvPI
Theme: 'Your Safety, Just a Click Away: Report to PvPI'
Stresses simple digital reporting by doctors and patients
Easy QR and online reporting lowers the effort barrier
Patients can report directly, widening the base beyond doctors
Wider medicine use and self-medication need continuous surveillance
Reports feed signal detection that premarketing trials cannot show
Lack of awareness of PvPI and how to report
Belief that an approved or well-known drug is safe
Fear of blame, litigation or loss of reputation
Mild or common reactions dismissed as expected
Time burden with no feedback or incentive to report
